doc.title: Joe LaBarbera interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 15, 2021

title: Replacing Gap Mangione in 1968 and landing an Army band post
summary: Joe took Gap's chair, was drafted, jammed with the 173rd Army Band at induction and stayed two years; his father's band teaching saved others in WWII.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: But then you replaced him in 1968 with Gap Mangione?

Yes. I took his place when he enlisted in the army, I took that gig, which only lasted a matter of months because I was drafted very quickly. This was 1968, right? But I got through my military service fortunately and came home and went back with Gap and then went out with Woody’s band.
I was curious about that if you got drafted or if you had enlisted. And gee at that time, how were you able to get out in two years?

With a lot of lobbying. I mean fortunately, this is kind of an interesting story. You arrive at the induction center in the dark of night, so you don’t know where you are, you’re completely disoriented, they stick you in a barracks. But as luck would have it the band that I would eventually be stationed in was in the induction center. So I hear guys playing to I immediately like snuck out of the barracks, went over and started jamming with these guys, and put myself on their radar from day one. So all the way through basic training I

was going over there, playing with these guys, you know, ingratiating myself as much as I could, and by the time we were given our orders after basic training, mine was to go to the 173rd Army Band in the induction center and that’s where I stayed for the next two years.
Well I can add that to quite a few stories we’ve heard from musicians who made their way through the military and sometimes escaped combat because that they were able to play and be versatile.

You know I go back to my father about this, because he taught generations of young boys in my hometown starting with the 30s, and I cannot tell you how many of these grown- ups would come to us later when we would meet them and they would say, “Your father saved my life during World War II because I was able to get into a band” here or there or wherever. So I was extremely fortunate, Monk.
